chapters.title: Part 1: Core Java Fundamentals
chapters.description: The essential building blocks of Java — your first program, data types, user input, arithmetic, and conditional logic.

slides.title: What is Java?
slides.content: Java is a compiled, platform-independent language that runs on any OS via the JVM.
bullets: Write Once, Run Anywhere — Java source compiles to bytecode that runs on any OS via the JVM
Strongly typed: every variable must be declared with a specific data type before it can be used
javac (the compiler) converts .java source files into .class bytecode files
The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) executes the bytecode — you never run .java files directly

slides.title: Setting Up Your Environment
slides.content: Install the JDK to compile Java and IntelliJ IDEA as your IDE.
bullets: Install the JDK (Java Development Kit) from oracle.com — includes javac (compiler) and the JVM runtime
Install IntelliJ IDEA Community Edition (free) as your IDE — it handles compile and run for you
In IntelliJ: New Project → select your JDK version → uncheck 'Add sample code'
Create a class named Main inside the src/ folder — the filename must always match the class name

slides.title: The main() Method — Entry Point
slides.content: Every Java program starts execution at main() — its exact signature is mandatory.
bullets: Java programs start at public static void main(String[] args) — this exact signature is required
public: accessible by the JVM;  static: called without creating an object;  void: returns nothing
Missing or misspelling main gives a runtime error: 'Main method not found in class Main'
Everything your program does lives inside the { } braces of main

slides.title: Printing to the Console
slides.content: System.out.println() and System.out.print() write text to the console output window.
bullets: System.out.println() prints text then moves the cursor to a new line automatically
System.out.print() prints text and keeps the cursor on the same line
Use the escape sequence \n inside a string to insert a manual line break anywhere
IntelliJ shortcut: type sout then press Tab to auto-generate System.out.println()

slides.title: Comments in Java
slides.content: Comments are notes in your code that the compiler completely ignores at compile time.
bullets: Single-line comment: // everything after this is ignored on this line
Multi-line comment: /* ... */ — useful for longer explanations spanning multiple lines
Comments are for humans — future you, teammates, your instructor — not the compiler
Commenting out code is a debugging trick: temporarily disable a line without deleting it

slides.title: What is a Variable?
slides.content: A variable is a named container in memory that holds a value you can use and update.
bullets: Declaration: state the data type and name — int age;
Assignment: give it a value — age = 21;
Combined (most common): int age = 21; — declares and assigns in one line
Primitive types (int, double, char, boolean) store the value directly; String stores a memory address

slides.title: int — Whole Numbers
slides.content: int stores whole numbers without a decimal portion — ideal for counts, ages, and quantities.
bullets: int holds whole numbers in the range -2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,647
Use int for ages, years, quantities, counts — anything guaranteed to be a whole number
Storing a decimal in an int causes a compile error: incompatible types
Tip: use underscores to make large numbers readable — 1_000_000 is the same as 1000000

slides.title: double — Decimal Numbers
slides.content: double stores 64-bit floating-point numbers — the default choice for any decimal value in Java.
bullets: double stores numbers with a decimal — use it for prices, GPAs, temperatures, measurements
Storing a whole number in a double adds .0 automatically — the value 5 becomes 5.0
Prefer double over float — double has 64-bit precision vs float's 32-bit, and is the Java default
float literals need an f suffix: 3.14f — without it Java treats the literal as a double

slides.title: char and boolean
slides.content: char holds a single character in single quotes; boolean holds exactly true or false.
bullets: char holds exactly one character — always use single quotes: 'A', not "A"
boolean holds true or false — represents yes/no, on/off, pass/fail states
Naming convention: boolean variables start with is, has, or can — isStudent, hasDiscount
Common mistake: 'A' is a char; "A" is a String — they are completely different types

slides.title: String — Text Data
slides.content: String is a reference type that stores a sequence of characters, always wrapped in double quotes.
bullets: String is a reference type (not primitive) — it stores a memory address pointing to heap data
Always use double quotes for Strings: "Hello" — single quotes are for char only
Concatenate (join) Strings with +: "Hello, " + name produces a combined String
You can concatenate any primitive with a String — Java converts the primitive to text automatically

slides.title: Naming Conventions & Best Practices
slides.content: Java uses camelCase for variables — descriptive names make code self-documenting.
bullets: Use camelCase for variable names: firstName, isStudent, totalPrice — first word lowercase, each subsequent word capitalised
Names must be descriptive — age beats a, userName beats un
Java is case-sensitive: myVar and MyVar are completely different variables
Constants (values that never change) are named ALL_CAPS with final: final int MAX_SIZE = 100;

slides.title: The Scanner Class
slides.content: Scanner is a Java class that reads keyboard input — import it before use and close it when done.
bullets: Add import java.util.Scanner; at the top of your file, before the class declaration
Create one Scanner connected to the keyboard: Scanner scanner = new Scanner(System.in);
System.in tells Scanner to read from standard input (the keyboard)
Always call scanner.close() at the end — leaving resources open causes unexpected behaviour

slides.title: Reading Strings and Integers
slides.content: Use nextLine() to read a full line of text and nextInt() to read a whole number.
bullets: scanner.nextLine() reads an entire line of text, including spaces — stops at Enter
scanner.next() reads one word only — stops at the first space character
scanner.nextInt() reads a whole number — entering a decimal causes InputMismatchException
Always prompt the user with System.out.print() before each scanner call

slides.title: Reading Doubles and Booleans
slides.content: Use nextDouble() for decimals and nextBoolean() for true/false keyboard input.
bullets: scanner.nextDouble() reads a decimal — entering a whole number is fine (stored as 3.0)
scanner.nextBoolean() reads true or false — case-insensitive: TRUE, True, and true all work
Entering the wrong type (letters when expecting a number) crashes with InputMismatchException
Always prompt clearly so the user knows whether to enter a number, word, or true/false

slides.title: The Newline Buffer Bug
slides.content: After nextInt() or nextDouble(), a leftover newline silently skips the next nextLine() call.
bullets: When you type a number and press Enter, the '\n' character stays in the input buffer
The next nextLine() immediately reads that leftover newline as an empty string and returns
Fix: call scanner.nextLine() once directly after nextInt() or nextDouble() to flush the buffer
This is one of the most common beginner bugs — watch for it whenever you mix input types

slides.title: Practice: Rectangle Area Calculator
slides.content: Build a program that accepts width and height from the user and calculates the rectangle's area.
bullets: Declare all variables at the top with initial values before collecting input
Standard flow: Prompt -> Accept -> Calculate -> Display
Use double for measurements to support decimal values like 3.5 cm
Multiply width x height to compute area — combine the result with a unit label in the output

slides.title: Mad Libs — Project Overview
slides.content: Mad Libs collects words from the user and slots them into a story template — great Scanner and concatenation practice.
bullets: Mad Libs: collect several words (adjective, noun, verb) then insert them into a pre-written story
This project combines Scanner input, String variables, and concatenation with +
An adjective describes something (fast, loud), a noun is a person/place/thing, a verb is an action
Plan your story template first, identify each blank, then code the input collection

slides.title: Building the Story
slides.content: Collect all words first, then print the completed story using String concatenation.
bullets: Declare all String variables before the first prompt to avoid 'variable not initialised' errors
Collect all input before printing — do not interleave prompts and story output
Build each story line: System.out.println("literal " + variable + " more text");
Close the Scanner after collecting all input, before printing the story

slides.title: Mad Libs — Challenge
slides.content: Extend Mad Libs with a number input and a second story line.
bullets: Write your own story template with at least 6 blanks — make it funny!
Add a number input using nextInt() — remember to flush the buffer with nextLine() afterwards
Include the number in the story: "I counted " + count + " wild " + animal + "(s) today!"
Try mixing nextInt() and nextLine() — this is exactly where the buffer bug appears

slides.title: Basic Arithmetic Operators
slides.content: Java supports five standard arithmetic operators — addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and modulus.
bullets: +  addition,  -  subtraction,  *  multiplication,  /  division,  %  modulus (remainder)
Store the result in a variable: int result = x + y;
All five operators work on both int and double — the result type matches the wider operand
The modulus operator % returns the remainder after division: 10 % 3 = 1
slides.code:
int x = 10, y = 3;

System.out.println(x + y);  // 13  — addition
System.out.println(x - y);  // 7   — subtraction
System.out.println(x * y);  // 30  — multiplication
System.out.println(x / y);  // 3   — integer division (see next slide)
System.out.println(x % y);  // 1   — remainder: 10 / 3 = 3 remainder 1

// Common use of % — check even or odd
System.out.println(10 % 2);  // 0 -> even
System.out.println(11 % 2);  // 1 -> odd

slides.title: Integer Division vs Double Division
slides.content: Dividing two ints truncates the decimal — use a double operand or a cast to keep the fractional part.
bullets: int / int performs integer division — the decimal is truncated, not rounded
10 / 3 = 3, not 3.33 — both operands are int so the result is an int
To keep the decimal, make at least one operand a double: 10 / 3.0 = 3.333...
Type casting: (double) x / y temporarily promotes x to double for this calculation

slides.title: Augmented Assignment Operators
slides.content: Augmented assignment operators update a variable in place — shorter syntax, same result.
bullets: x += 5 is the same as x = x + 5 — updates x using its own current value
The variable on the left is both read (old value) and overwritten (new value)
Commonly used inside loops to accumulate a running total or counter

slides.title: Increment & Decrement
slides.content: ++ and -- add or subtract exactly 1 — the most concise update operators in Java.
bullets: x++ adds 1 to x — equivalent to x += 1 and x = x + 1
x-- subtracts 1 from x — equivalent to x -= 1
Each ++ or -- permanently changes the value stored in x
You will see i++ in virtually every for loop — it is the most common use

slides.title: Order of Operations (PEMDAS)
slides.content: Java follows standard mathematical precedence — use parentheses to make intent explicit.
bullets: Evaluation order: Parentheses -> Multiply/Divide -> Add/Subtract (left to right within each tier)
Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction
When in doubt, add parentheses — they cost nothing and prevent silent bugs
Integer division within a larger expression still truncates — always check your operand types

slides.title: Shopping Cart — Project Overview
slides.content: Build a program that collects an item, price, and quantity from the user and prints a formatted total.
bullets: Collect three inputs: item name (String), price per unit (double), quantity (int)
Total = price x quantity — simple multiplication of two user-provided values
Use a char for the currency symbol so you can swap $ to EUR without changing every print line
This project applies Scanner, data types, arithmetic, and String concatenation together

slides.title: Collecting Input & Computing Total
slides.content: Prompt for each value in sequence, then multiply price by quantity to get the total.
bullets: Use System.out.print() for prompts — keeps the cursor on the same line as user input
After all inputs are collected, compute: total = price * quantity
Display the formatted receipt using concatenation — include the currency char on each line
Declare variables before Scanner calls — avoids 'variable not initialised' errors

slides.title: Shopping Cart — Challenge
slides.content: Extend the cart to support two items and apply a 10% discount when the total exceeds $50.
bullets: Compute a grand total: grandTotal = (price1 * qty1) + (price2 * qty2)
Apply a 10% discount conditionally: if (grandTotal > 50) grandTotal *= 0.90;
This preview uses an if statement — the next lesson covers if in full detail
Try adding a third item: repeating code starts to feel wrong — loops solve this (coming soon)

slides.title: The if Statement
slides.content: An if statement executes a block of code only when its condition evaluates to true.
bullets: Syntax: if (condition) { // code that runs only when condition is true }
The condition must be a boolean expression — something that evaluates to true or false
If the condition is false, the entire block is skipped — no error, just ignored
Comparison operators: == (equal)  !=  >  <  >=  <=

slides.title: else and else if
slides.content: else provides a fallback when if is false; else if checks additional conditions in sequence.
bullets: else runs when the if condition is false — it is the default fallback branch
else if checks a second condition only if all previous conditions were false
Only ONE branch ever executes — Java evaluates top-to-bottom and stops at the first true match
The final else (no condition) catches everything not matched by any if or else if above

slides.title: Comparison Operators
slides.content: Comparison operators produce a boolean result — use double == for equality, never single =.
bullets: == checks equality (double equals) — single = is assignment and causes a compile error in a condition
!= means 'not equal to'
> greater than,  < less than,  >= greater or equal,  <= less or equal
For Strings use .equals() not == : name.equals("Alice") — == on Strings compares references, not content

slides.title: Booleans as Conditions
slides.content: A boolean variable is already a condition — no need to compare it with == true.
bullets: if (isStudent) is identical to if (isStudent == true) — the shorter form is preferred
Use ! (logical NOT) to negate: if (!isStudent) means 'if NOT a student'
&& (AND) requires both sides true;  || (OR) requires at least one side true
Boolean flags are the standard way to track state — is something on, available, or active?

chapters.title: Part 2: Java Tools & Techniques
chapters.description: Random numbers, the Math class, formatted output with printf, nested conditions, and String methods.

slides.title: Importing and Creating a Random Object
slides.content: The Random class generates pseudo-random numbers — import and instantiate it like Scanner.
bullets: Add import java.util.Random; at the top of your file, before the class declaration
Create one Random object: Random random = new Random();
The Random class follows the same import-instantiate-use pattern as Scanner
Random numbers are pseudo-random — generated by a deterministic algorithm seeded from the clock

slides.title: nextInt() — Integers in a Range
slides.content: nextInt(bound) generates an integer from 0 inclusive to bound exclusive.
bullets: random.nextInt(bound) returns 0 to bound-1 — the bound itself is never returned
Simulating a 6-sided die (1-6): random.nextInt(6) + 1
The + 1 shifts the range: without it you get 0-5, with it you get 1-6
General range min to max: random.nextInt(max - min + 1) + min

slides.title: nextDouble() and nextBoolean()
slides.content: nextDouble() produces a decimal from 0.0 to just below 1.0; nextBoolean() gives random true or false.
bullets: random.nextDouble() returns a double from 0.0 (inclusive) to 1.0 (exclusive)
Scale to a range: random.nextDouble() * 100.0 gives 0.0 to 99.9...
random.nextBoolean() returns true or false with equal 50% probability
Use nextBoolean() to simulate coin flips, random yes/no decisions, or toggle flags

slides.title: Practice: Dice Roller
slides.content: Roll two dice, sum them, and announce whether the total is a winning 7.
bullets: Roll each die separately: random.nextInt(6) + 1 gives values 1-6
Sum the two results — two dice produce totals from 2 to 12
Print both individual rolls and the combined total
A total of 7 wins — use an if statement to announce the result

slides.title: Math Constants — PI and E
slides.content: The Math class provides built-in constants and methods — no import required.
bullets: Math is in java.lang — auto-imported, no import statement needed
Math.PI holds pi (3.14159...) as a double constant
Math.E holds Euler's number (2.71828...) used in natural logarithms
Always prefix with Math. and use UPPERCASE: Math.PI, Math.E

slides.title: Rounding — round(), ceil(), floor()
slides.content: Java provides three distinct rounding behaviours through the Math class.
bullets: Math.round(x) rounds to the nearest whole number — .5 rounds up — returns a long
Math.ceil(x) always rounds UP to the next whole number — returns a double
Math.floor(x) always rounds DOWN to the previous whole number — returns a double
For negatives: ceil(-2.9) = -2.0, floor(-2.9) = -3.0 — ceiling is closer to zero
slides.code:
double x = 3.6, y = 3.4;

System.out.println(Math.round(x));  // 4   — nearest
System.out.println(Math.round(y));  // 3   — nearest
System.out.println(Math.ceil(y));   // 4.0 — always up
System.out.println(Math.floor(x));  // 3.0 — always down

// Negative values:
System.out.println(Math.ceil(-2.9));   // -2.0 — up toward zero
System.out.println(Math.floor(-2.9));  // -3.0 — down away from zero

slides.title: pow(), sqrt(), abs(), max(), min()
slides.content: The five most-used Math methods in everyday Java programming.
bullets: Math.pow(base, exp) raises base to the power of exp — returns a double
Math.sqrt(x) returns the square root of x as a double
Math.abs(x) returns the absolute value — strips the negative sign
Math.max(a, b) and Math.min(a, b) return the larger or smaller of two values
slides.code:
System.out.println(Math.pow(2, 10));    // 1024.0  (2^10)
System.out.println(Math.pow(9, 0.5));   // 3.0     (square root via pow)
System.out.println(Math.sqrt(144));     // 12.0
System.out.println(Math.abs(-47));      // 47
System.out.println(Math.abs(-3.14));    // 3.14

System.out.println(Math.max(18, 25));   // 25
System.out.println(Math.min(18, 25));   // 18

slides.title: Practice: Hypotenuse Calculator
slides.content: Apply Math.pow() and Math.sqrt() to compute the hypotenuse of a right triangle.
bullets: Pythagorean theorem: c = sqrt(a^2 + b^2)
Math.pow(a, 2) squares side a — add both, then take Math.sqrt()
Accept a and b from the user with Scanner
printf with %.2f rounds the result to two decimal places

slides.title: Why printf?
slides.content: System.out.printf() formats output precisely — controlling decimal places, field widths, and variable placement.
bullets: printf = print formatted — inserts variables into a template string via % placeholders
Placeholders: %s (String), %d (int), %f (double), %c (char), %b (boolean)
printf does NOT add a newline — use %n (or \n) at the end of the format string
Prefer printf over concatenation when you need precise alignment or decimal control

slides.title: Format Specifiers — %s, %d, %c, %b
slides.content: Each data type has a corresponding format specifier character in printf.
bullets: %s — String (any object converted to text)
%d — integer (int or long) — stands for decimal integer
%c — char — displays a single character
%b — boolean — displays true or false

slides.title: Double Precision — %f and %.2f
slides.content: Use %f for doubles — control decimal places with a dot-precision modifier.
bullets: %f displays a double with 6 decimal places by default
%.2f limits the output to exactly 2 decimal places — standard for prices
%.0f rounds to the nearest whole number with no decimal point shown
Modifier syntax: %.Nf where N is the number of decimal places

slides.title: Width and Alignment
slides.content: A width number reserves a minimum field size — use - for left-alignment.
bullets: %10d reserves 10 characters and right-aligns the integer
%-10s reserves 10 characters and left-aligns the String (minus = left)
Width is the minimum field — content wider than width is not truncated
Combine width and precision: %10.2f = 10 chars wide, 2 decimal places

slides.title: Practice: Formatted Receipt
slides.content: Use printf to print a shopping receipt with aligned item names and right-justified prices.
bullets: Left-align item names with %-20s, right-align prices with $%6.2f
Use a separator line of dashes for visual structure
Compute the total and display it with the same alignment
This table pattern appears in real-world billing, banking, and report code

slides.title: Project: Compound Interest
slides.content: Apply Math.pow() and printf to a real-world finance formula.
bullets: Compound interest grows on both the principal and previously earned interest
Formula: A = P * (1 + r/n)^(n*t)
P = principal, r = annual rate as decimal, n = compoundings per year, t = years
A is the final amount — A minus P gives the total interest earned

slides.title: Applying Math.pow()
slides.content: Math.pow() handles the exponentiation — watch integer division in the base.
bullets: Math.pow(1 + r/n, n*t) computes the growth factor
r is a double, n is an int — r/n is double/int which gives a double result (safe)
Multiply the result by P to get the final amount A
printf with %.2f displays the dollar amounts cleanly

slides.title: Compound Interest — Challenge
slides.content: Compare monthly vs annual compounding side by side to see the difference.
bullets: Run the formula twice: once with n=12 (monthly), once with n=1 (annual)
Display both final amounts and the difference between them
The gap shows why banks advertise compounding frequency — it matters
Challenge: compute how many years to double the money: t = ln(2) / (n * ln(1 + r/n))

slides.title: if Inside an if
slides.content: A nested if checks a secondary condition only after the primary condition is already true.
bullets: A nested if is placed inside the body of another if — it acts as a second gate
The inner if runs only when the outer if condition is true
Each nesting level adds one indentation level — limit to 2-3 levels for readability
Use nesting when condition B only makes sense if condition A is already satisfied

slides.title: Nesting vs else-if — When to Choose
slides.content: Choose else-if for independent alternatives; choose nesting when condition B depends on condition A.
bullets: Use else-if when conditions are independent alternatives — only one branch runs
Use nesting when condition B is meaningless unless condition A is already true
Deeply nested code is hard to read — flatten with && when possible
if (a && b) { } is usually cleaner than if (a) { if (b) { } } for simple cases

slides.title: Practice: Grade Classifier
slides.content: Use nested conditions to validate input then classify a score into a letter grade.
bullets: Outer condition: validate the score is in range (0-100)
Inner else-if chain: A >= 90, B >= 80, C >= 70, D >= 60, F otherwise
A second nested if can flag a distinction for scores >= 90
Validate first, classify second — this two-gate pattern mirrors real eligibility logic

slides.title: Case and Length
slides.content: String methods are called with a dot after the variable — they return new Strings, leaving the original unchanged.
bullets: str.toUpperCase() returns a new String with all letters capitalised
str.toLowerCase() returns a new String with all letters lowercased
str.length() returns the number of characters as an int — spaces and punctuation count
String methods never modify the original — reassign the variable to keep the change

slides.title: charAt() and indexOf()
slides.content: charAt() reads one character by position; indexOf() finds the first position of a character or substring.
bullets: str.charAt(index) returns the char at the given zero-based index
Strings are zero-indexed: "Hello".charAt(0) = 'H', charAt(4) = 'o'
str.indexOf('x') returns the first index of character x, or -1 if not found
str.indexOf("sub") finds the starting index of the first occurrence of a substring
slides.code:
String word  = "Hello";
String email = "user@example.com";

System.out.println(word.charAt(0));       // H
System.out.println(word.charAt(4));       // o

System.out.println(email.indexOf('@'));   // 4
System.out.println(email.indexOf("ex"));  // 5
System.out.println(email.indexOf('z'));   // -1 (not found)

slides.title: contains(), isEmpty(), replace(), trim()
slides.content: Four essential methods for searching, checking, and cleaning String values.
bullets: str.contains("x") returns true if the string contains the substring x anywhere
str.isEmpty() returns true if the string has zero characters — same as length() == 0
str.replace("old", "new") returns a new String with every occurrence swapped
str.trim() removes leading and trailing whitespace — essential for cleaning user input
slides.code:
String pwd = "secure123";

System.out.println(pwd.contains("123"));  // true
System.out.println(pwd.contains("xyz"));  // false
System.out.println("".isEmpty());         // true
System.out.println(pwd.isEmpty());        // false

String s = "I like cats and cats.".replace("cats", "dogs");
System.out.println(s);  // I like dogs and dogs.

System.out.println("   hello   ".trim());  // hello

slides.title: equals() and equalsIgnoreCase()
slides.content: Never use == to compare String content — always use .equals() or .equalsIgnoreCase().
bullets: str.equals(other) returns true when both strings have identical characters
== on Strings compares memory addresses, not content — it is unreliable for comparison
str.equalsIgnoreCase(other) compares content ignoring uppercase/lowercase differences
Use equalsIgnoreCase() for user input — users may type YES, yes, or Yes

slides.title: The substring() Method
slides.content: substring() extracts a portion of a String using start and end indices.
bullets: str.substring(start) returns everything from index start to the end
str.substring(start, end) returns characters from start up to but NOT including end
Indices are zero-based — first character is at index 0
Pair with indexOf() to extract dynamic portions like the domain of an email

slides.title: Email Slicer — Design
slides.content: The @ character separates username from domain — indexOf() finds it, substring() splits on it.
bullets: indexOf('@') locates the @ symbol position
Username: substring(0, atIndex) — everything before the @
Domain: substring(atIndex + 1) — everything after the @
Validate @ exists first: if indexOf returns -1, the email is malformed

slides.title: Email Slicer — Challenge
slides.content: Extend the slicer to also extract the TLD and validate minimum username length.
bullets: lastIndexOf('.') finds the final dot — use it to extract the TLD (.com, .org)
TLD: email.substring(lastDotIndex + 1)
Validate username: if (username.length() < 3) warn the user
Check domain contains at least one dot — indexOf('.') on domain != -1

chapters.title: Part 3: Control Flow & Loops
chapters.description: Ternary operator, enhanced switch statements, logical operators, and your first loops.

slides.title: Pseudocode First
slides.content: Write the program plan as comments before any code — pseudocode makes complex programs manageable.
bullets: Pseudocode: write your program steps as plain-English comments before touching Java syntax
Steps: 1) declare variables  2) welcome message  3) prompt for choice  4) convert  5) display
Two options: 1 = pounds to kg,  2 = kg to pounds — anything else is invalid
This project uses: Scanner, double, int, if/else, and arithmetic

slides.title: Conversion Formulas
slides.content: Pounds to kg divides by 2.205; kg to pounds multiplies by 2.205.
bullets: 1 pound = 0.453592 kg — equivalently: kg = lbs / 2.205
1 kg = 2.20462 lbs — equivalently: lbs = kg * 2.205
Store the factor as a constant: final double FACTOR = 2.205;
printf with %.2f is standard for weight — two decimal places

slides.title: Full Weight Converter
slides.content: The complete weight converter — all pieces assembled.
bullets: Prompt for choice first, then prompt for the weight value — ordering matters for UX
nextInt() for choice, then nextDouble() for weight — no buffer flush needed between them
printf formats both the input and converted values on the same output line
Challenge: add option 3 for stone to kg (1 stone = 6.35 kg)

slides.title: Ternary Syntax
slides.content: The ternary operator is a compact one-line if/else that resolves to a value.
bullets: Syntax: condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse
The result can be assigned to a variable or passed directly into println/printf
Read it as: condition is true? use A, otherwise use B
Ternary is NOT a general replacement for if/else — it only resolves to a single expression

slides.title: When to Use Ternary
slides.content: Ternary shines for simple label or value selection — avoid nesting ternaries inside ternaries.
bullets: Great for: labelling (odd/even, pass/fail, yes/no, online/offline)
Great for: picking one of two simple values based on a single condition
Avoid: nested ternaries — they are nearly impossible to read and debug
Avoid: ternaries with side effects — ternary is for selecting a value, not running logic

slides.title: Ternary Inside println and printf
slides.content: Embed ternary directly inside print statements for compact conditional output.
bullets: You can nest a ternary expression as an argument to println or printf
This is common in logging and diagnostic output where labels depend on state
Keep the condition simple — if it needs explaining, use if/else instead
Ternary resolves to one value — it cannot replace multi-statement if/else blocks

slides.title: Project: Temperature Converter
slides.content: Build a two-direction temperature converter — C to F or F to C.
bullets: Two directions: Celsius to Fahrenheit, and Fahrenheit to Celsius
Accept the unit as a String input — use toUpperCase() so C or c both work
Use if/else to branch to the correct formula
This project combines: Scanner, String methods, double, if/else, and printf

slides.title: Celsius and Fahrenheit Formulas
slides.content: Two formulas, one for each direction — use 9.0/5.0 not 9/5 to avoid integer division.
bullets: Celsius to Fahrenheit: F = C * (9.0 / 5.0) + 32
Fahrenheit to Celsius: C = (F - 32) * (5.0 / 9.0)
Use 9.0 and 5.0 not 9 and 5 — integer division 9/5 = 1, not 1.8
printf with %.1f shows one decimal place — standard for temperature display

slides.title: Temperature Converter — Challenge
slides.content: Extend the converter to support Kelvin as a third unit.
bullets: Kelvin to Celsius: C = K - 273.15
Celsius to Kelvin: K = C + 273.15
Add a third else-if branch: else if (unit.equals("K"))
Kelvin has no negatives — validate: if (temp < 0 && unit.equals("K")) print an error

slides.title: What is a Switch?
slides.content: A switch statement is a cleaner alternative to long else-if chains when comparing one variable against many fixed values.
bullets: switch examines one variable and jumps to the matching case — cleaner than 10+ else-if blocks
Java 14 introduced enhanced switch — preferred over classic switch
Classic switch uses colon + break — forgetting break causes fall-through to the next case
Strings, ints, chars, and enums all work as the switch subject

slides.title: Enhanced Switch Syntax (Java 14+)
slides.content: Enhanced switch uses -> arrows — no fall-through, no break needed.
bullets: Enhanced switch: case "x" -> doSomething(); — stops automatically after each case
Multiple values share one case: case "Sat", "Sun" -> System.out.println("Weekend!");
The default case handles anything not matched by a named case
Enhanced switch can also be an expression — assign its result to a variable

slides.title: Multi-line Switch Cases with yield
slides.content: When a case needs multiple statements, wrap them in braces and use yield to return a value.
bullets: Single-statement case: case "x" -> value;
Multi-statement case: case "x" -> { doA(); doB(); yield value; }
yield is used inside switch expression blocks to return the value for that case
Keep cases short — extract complex logic into a method and call it from the case

slides.title: switch vs else-if — When to Choose
slides.content: Switch is preferred for 3+ fixed values against one variable — else-if for complex boolean conditions.
bullets: Use switch when comparing one variable against 3+ known constant values
Use else-if when conditions involve ranges, multiple variables, or complex logic
switch (score) cannot do >= 90 — ranges require else-if or nesting
Enhanced switch is also more efficient — the JVM can compile it to a jump table

slides.title: Project: Calculator with Enhanced Switch
slides.content: Build a four-operation calculator — enhanced switch selects the operation.
bullets: Accept two numbers and an operator (+, -, *, /) from the user
Use enhanced switch on the operator String to route to the correct calculation
Guard against division by zero: print an error if the divisor is 0
Display the result with printf using %.2f for decimal formatting

slides.title: Switch on the Operator
slides.content: Route to the correct arithmetic operation using an enhanced switch on the operator string.
bullets: Switch on the operator String: case "+" ->, case "-" ->, case "*" ->, case "/" ->
Division needs a zero guard: check b != 0 before dividing
The default case catches any unrecognised symbol and flags it as unknown
Track a valid flag to decide whether to print the result

slides.title: Calculator — Challenge
slides.content: Add modulus and power operators, then wrap the whole program in a loop.
bullets: Add case "%" -> result = a % b; for remainder
Add case "^" -> result = Math.pow(a, b); for exponentiation
Wrap the input and switch in a while(true) loop — add a quit option (q)
Break out with break when the user types q — this is the standard REPL pattern

slides.title: && — The AND Operator
slides.content: && combines two conditions — the result is true only when BOTH sides are true.
bullets: condition1 && condition2 is true only when both conditions are true simultaneously
Short-circuit: if condition1 is false, Java skips condition2 entirely
Use && to enforce multiple requirements: logged in AND is an admin
Truth table: T&&T=T, T&&F=F, F&&T=F, F&&F=F

slides.title: || and ! — OR and NOT
slides.content: || is true when at least one side is true; ! inverts any boolean value.
bullets: condition1 || condition2 is true if EITHER or BOTH conditions are true
Short-circuit: if condition1 is true, Java skips condition2
! inverts a boolean: !true = false, !false = true
Combine && and || with parentheses to control evaluation order

slides.title: Combining Operators — Precedence
slides.content: && binds tighter than || — always use parentheses when mixing them.
bullets: && has higher precedence than || — a || b && c means a || (b && c)
Always add parentheses when mixing && and || to make intent unambiguous
Chaining: (a && b && c) all three must be true; (a || b || c) at least one
De Morgan's law: !(a && b) equals (!a || !b) — useful for simplifying negated conditions

slides.title: The while Loop
slides.content: A while loop repeats a block of code as long as its condition remains true.
bullets: Syntax: while (condition) { // repeated code }
Condition is checked BEFORE each iteration — if false from the start, body never runs
You must update something inside the loop that eventually makes the condition false
while loops are ideal when you do not know in advance how many times to repeat

slides.title: Infinite Loops — Avoiding Them
slides.content: A loop whose condition never becomes false runs forever and freezes your program.
bullets: Infinite loop: the condition is never updated to false inside the body
Common causes: forgetting i++, wrong condition direction, or an unreachable exit
Intentional loop: while (true) { ... } — must exit with break or return
If the program freezes: hit the red Stop button in IntelliJ or press Ctrl+C in the terminal

slides.title: do-while Loop
slides.content: do-while runs the body at least once, then checks the condition.
bullets: Syntax: do { // code } while (condition);  — note the semicolon after the closing parenthesis
Body executes FIRST, condition checked AFTER — guaranteed at least one iteration
Use do-while when the first run must always happen regardless of the condition
Classic use: menu loops — show the menu at least once, repeat until the user quits

slides.title: Practice: Input Validation Loop
slides.content: Use a while loop to keep prompting the user until they enter a valid value.
bullets: Initialise the variable to an invalid value so the loop starts: int age = -1;
Loop condition: while the value is outside the valid range, keep asking
Print an error message inside the loop to guide the user
Input validation is essential for any real program — never assume the user enters correct data

chapters.title: Part 4: For Loops & Arrays
chapters.description: Master the for loop and Java arrays — the backbone of data iteration and collection.

slides.title: For Loop Syntax
slides.content: A for loop compresses counter setup, condition, and update into one line — use it when the iteration count is known.
bullets: Syntax: for (initialiser; condition; update) { // body } — three sections separated by semicolons
The initialiser runs once; the condition is checked before each iteration; the update runs after each body execution
Conventional counter variable: int i = 0 — 'i' is shorthand for index, universally understood
When the condition is false, the loop exits and execution continues after the closing brace

slides.title: Counting Down & Step Sizes
slides.content: Change the initialiser and update expression to count backwards or skip values.
bullets: Count down: start high, condition >= 1, decrement with i-- — for (int i = 5; i >= 1; i--)
Skip values: i += 2 steps by 2 — produces 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 from a single loop
The update expression can be any valid statement — i += 10, i *= 2, or i = i + 3
Counting direction and step size are independent — increment or decrement by any amount

slides.title: for vs while — When to Choose
slides.content: Use for when the iteration count is known up front; use while when the exit condition depends on runtime state.
bullets: Use for when you know exactly how many iterations are needed: 5 times, N times, array.length times
Use while when the exit depends on user input, a search result, or other data known only at runtime
A for loop compiles to the same bytecode as an equivalent while loop — it is a style and readability choice
Both for and while support break (exit early) and continue (skip to the next iteration)

slides.title: break and continue
slides.content: break exits the loop immediately; continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the update.
bullets: break: immediately exits the loop — execution resumes after the closing brace
continue: skips the remainder of this iteration and jumps to the update expression (i++)
Use break to stop early once a target is found; use continue to skip unwanted values
Overusing break and continue in complex loops makes code hard to follow — prefer a clear condition

slides.title: Nested Loop Concept
slides.content: A nested loop places one for loop inside another — the inner loop runs fully for each single outer iteration.
bullets: The inner loop runs completely from start to finish for every single iteration of the outer loop
Use distinct counter names: outer i, inner j — never reuse the same variable in both loops
Total iterations = outer count × inner count — a 3×3 nested loop executes 9 times total
Nesting more than 2 levels deep usually signals the logic should be extracted into a method

slides.title: Multiplication Table
slides.content: A 10×10 multiplication table is the classic nested loop exercise — outer loop is the row, inner is the column multiplier.
bullets: Outer loop: row 1-10; inner loop: column multiplier 1-10
Cell value: i * j — row i times column j gives the table entry at that position
printf with %4d right-aligns each number in a 4-character field, keeping columns neat
Call System.out.println() after the inner loop ends to move the cursor to the next row

slides.title: Triangle Pattern
slides.content: Tie the inner loop's upper bound to the outer counter to print shapes where each row has a different item count.
bullets: Setting the inner condition to j <= i prints one more star per row — row 1: 1 star, row N: N stars
This 'inner bound equals outer counter' pattern is the standard way to draw triangle shapes
Inverted triangle: reverse the outer loop (count i downward from rows to 1) and keep j <= i
The pattern is a classic interview question — practise explaining it step by step

slides.title: Project: Guessing Game Overview
slides.content: The guessing game picks a secret random number and loops until the player finds it, counting every attempt.
bullets: Random picks a secret integer from 1 to 100 — the player guesses until they match it
Use a while loop — the number of guesses is unknown in advance, so for is not appropriate
Track attempts with an int counter incremented on each guess
Give directional feedback after each wrong guess: Too high!, Too low!, or Correct!

slides.title: Game Loop & Feedback
slides.content: The while loop repeats until the guess matches the secret — counter tracks attempts automatically.
bullets: Initialise guess = 0 before the loop so the variable is in scope for the while condition
Loop condition: while (guess != secret) — the loop exits automatically on a correct guess
Increment counter inside the loop — after the loop ends, it holds the exact attempt count
Use if/else-if to give feedback: Too low, Too high, or Correct after each guess

slides.title: Challenge — Add a Guess Limit
slides.content: Extend the game with a maximum attempts cap and a win/lose outcome.
bullets: Add int maxGuesses = 7; and update the condition: while (guess != secret && counter < maxGuesses)
Track a boolean won flag — set it true when the guess matches the secret
After the loop: if (!won) reveal the secret and print 'Game over!'
Challenge: add difficulty levels — Easy = 10 guesses, Medium = 7, Hard = 5 — via a Scanner menu

slides.title: What is an Array?
slides.content: An array is a fixed-size, ordered collection of values all sharing one type and one variable name.
bullets: Declare: int[] scores; — type followed by [] then the variable name
Allocate: scores = new int[5]; — reserves space for exactly 5 integers in memory
Combined (most common): int[] scores = new int[5]; — declares and allocates in one line
Size is fixed at creation — you cannot add or remove slots after an array is made

slides.title: Indexing and Assignment
slides.content: Arrays are zero-indexed — the first element is at index 0, the last is at length-1.
bullets: Access an element: scores[0] = 95; — square brackets with the zero-based index
A 5-element array has valid indices 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — index 5 does not exist
Accessing an out-of-bounds index throws ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at runtime
array.length gives the element count — always use it instead of hardcoding the size

slides.title: Array Initialiser Syntax
slides.content: Declare, allocate, and fill an array in one line using a curly-brace initialiser.
bullets: int[] nums = {10, 20, 30, 40, 50}; — declares, allocates, and fills in a single statement
The size is inferred from the number of values — no need to write new int[5] separately
Works for any type: String[] days = {"Mon", "Tue", "Wed", "Thu", "Fri"};
Elements remain mutable after initialisation — you can still overwrite any index at any time

slides.title: Iterating an Array with for
slides.content: Loop from index 0 to array.length-1 to visit every element — use strictly less-than, not less-than-or-equal.
bullets: Standard pattern: for (int i = 0; i < arr.length; i++) — condition is strictly less than
Using <= arr.length causes ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException on the final iteration
Inside the loop, arr[i] gives the current value and i gives its position
Use indexed for when you need both the value and position; use for-each when only the value is needed

slides.title: Enhanced for Syntax
slides.content: The for-each loop iterates every element of an array without requiring an index variable.
bullets: Syntax: for (type element : array) { // use element } — reads as 'for each int in scores'
No index variable needed — cleaner and less error-prone than the standard indexed for loop
The element variable is a copy of each value — assigning to it does NOT change the original array
Works with any array type and, later, any Java Collection (ArrayList, Set, etc.)

slides.title: for-each vs for — When to Choose
slides.content: Default to for-each for reading values; switch to indexed for when you need the position or must modify elements.
bullets: for-each: cleaner, no off-by-one risk — preferred whenever you only need the values
Indexed for: required when you need the index, want to modify contents, or must traverse backwards
Assigning to the for-each variable only changes the local copy — the original array is unaffected
Rule of thumb: start with for-each, switch to indexed for only when the index is genuinely needed

slides.title: What is a 2D Array?
slides.content: A 2D array is an array of arrays — think of it as a grid with rows and columns.
bullets: Declare: int[][] grid = new int[3][4]; — 3 rows, 4 columns, 12 cells total
Access: grid[row][col] — row index first, then column index
grid.length gives the row count; grid[0].length gives the column count of the first row
Initialiser: int[][] m = {{1,2},{3,4},{5,6}}; — each inner {} block is one row

slides.title: Traversing a 2D Array
slides.content: Use nested for loops — the outer loop iterates rows, the inner loop iterates columns within each row.
bullets: Outer loop: for (int r = 0; r < grid.length; r++) — one pass per row
Inner loop: for (int c = 0; c < grid[r].length; c++) — one pass per column in that row
grid[r][c] reads or writes the element at row r, column c
Call System.out.println() after the inner loop to advance the display to the next row

slides.title: Practice: Seating Chart
slides.content: Model a cinema seating grid as a 2D char array — O for open seats, X for taken.
bullets: char[][] seats = new char[rows][cols]; — a grid of characters is perfect for a seat map
Fill all seats as open with nested for loops: seats[r][c] = 'O';
Mark specific seats as taken: seats[0][2] = 'X'; — direct index assignment
Real-world 2D arrays: image pixel grids, spreadsheet cells, chess/game boards

slides.title: Arrays.sort() and Arrays.toString()
slides.content: The Arrays utility class provides sort and display helpers — add import java.util.Arrays before using them.
bullets: Arrays.sort(arr) sorts in ascending order in-place — it permanently modifies the original array
Arrays.toString(arr) converts an array to a readable string like [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9]
Without Arrays.toString(), printing an array directly gives a useless memory address like [I@6d06d69c
Import: import java.util.Arrays; — Arrays is in java.util and must be imported, unlike Math

slides.title: Finding Min and Max
slides.content: Iterate the array to track the smallest and largest values seen — initialise both to the first element.
bullets: Initialise min and max to the first element: int min = arr[0]; int max = arr[0];
Start the loop from index 1 — index 0 is already the initial reference
Update min when a smaller value appears: if (arr[i] < min) min = arr[i];
After the loop, min and max hold the final answer — no sorting required

slides.title: Linear Search
slides.content: Linear search scans every element until the target is found — returns the index, or -1 if the value is absent.
bullets: Loop through each element; if arr[i] equals the target, return i immediately
Return -1 when the loop ends without a match — -1 is the universal 'not found' sentinel
Linear search works on unsorted arrays; binary search is faster but requires sorted input
Time complexity O(n) — in the worst case every element is checked before concluding absence

chapters.title: Part 5: Methods
chapters.description: Break programs into reusable, named methods — the foundation of structured and maintainable Java code.

slides.title: What is a Method?
slides.content: A method is a named, reusable block of code — call it by name to run its body from anywhere in the class.
bullets: A method packages code under a name so you can run it anywhere by calling that name
Without methods every program lives in main() — repetition, no structure, hard to maintain
Syntax: static void methodName() { // body } — static lets main() call it without creating an object
Call it: methodName(); — the JVM jumps to the method, runs it, then returns to the caller

slides.title: void Methods & Naming Conventions
slides.content: void means the method performs an action but produces no return value — name methods with action verbs.
bullets: void = 'this method produces no value' — it performs an action then exits
Use camelCase starting with a verb: printMenu(), displayResults(), rollDice()
Methods live inside the class but outside main() — they are siblings of main, not nested inside it
A method can call other methods — this is how programs build complex behaviour from simple parts

slides.title: Execution Flow
slides.content: When a method is called, execution jumps to it and returns to the caller when the method body ends.
bullets: The JVM pauses the caller, jumps to the called method, runs it top to bottom, then resumes the caller
The call stack is the record of which methods are paused and waiting to resume
Methods can call other methods — each is pushed onto and eventually popped from the call stack
A void method ends when it reaches its closing brace; a return; statement exits early

slides.title: Parameters — Passing Data In
slides.content: Parameters let callers pass data into a method — declared as typed variables inside the parentheses.
bullets: Parameter: the variable declared in the method signature — static void greet(String name)
Argument: the actual value passed at the call site — greet("Alice");
Parameters are local to the method — they do not exist outside it
Multiple parameters are listed comma-separated: static void add(int a, int b)

slides.title: Multiple Parameters & Pass by Value
slides.content: Java passes primitives by value — the method receives a copy, so modifying it never affects the caller's variable.
bullets: When you pass an int, a copy of the value is made — changing it inside the method has no effect outside
Pass by value means the caller's variable is never modified by a method that receives a primitive
Multiple parameters: list them comma-separated — static void display(String name, int score)
Argument order must match parameter order — Java matches by position, not by name

slides.title: Return Types & the return Statement
slides.content: Replace void with a type to declare that the method produces a value — return sends it back to the caller.
bullets: Replace void with the return type: static int add(int a, int b) promises to return an int
The return statement ends the method immediately and sends the value back to the caller
Every non-void code path must reach a return statement — missing one is a compile error
The caller receives the value: int result = add(5, 3); stores it for later use

slides.title: String and boolean Return Types
slides.content: Methods can return any type — String, double, boolean — not just numeric primitives.
bullets: static boolean isEven(int n) can return the expression n % 2 == 0 directly
static String getGrade(int score) builds and returns a grade label String
A method can return early — if a condition is met, return before the final line
A void method can use return; (no value) to exit early — the semicolon is required

slides.title: Practice: Temperature Converter as Methods
slides.content: Refactor the temperature formulas into dedicated methods — encapsulate once, call anywhere.
bullets: static double celsiusToFahrenheit(double c) returns c * (9.0 / 5.0) + 32
static double fahrenheitToCelsius(double f) returns (f - 32) * (5.0 / 9.0)
Caller: double f = celsiusToFahrenheit(100.0); — readable and reusable
Getting the formula right once in a method means it can never drift out of sync across the program

slides.title: Method Overloading
slides.content: Two methods can share a name if their parameter lists differ — Java picks the correct overload at compile time.
bullets: Method signature = name + parameter types — overloading means same name, different parameter list
Java selects the matching overload at compile time based on the argument types you pass
You cannot overload by return type alone — the parameter list must differ
Overloading gives callers a natural API: add(int, int), add(double, double), add(int, int, int)

slides.title: When to Use Overloading
slides.content: Overload when the same logical operation makes sense for multiple input types — avoid overloading unrelated logic.
bullets: Good use: print(String), print(int), print(double) — same action, different input types
Bad use: methods that do entirely different things under the same name — use distinct names instead
Java's System.out.println is itself a set of overloads — one for each common type
Overloaded methods are resolved at compile time — there is no runtime performance cost

slides.title: Local Scope
slides.content: A variable declared inside a method exists only for that method's lifetime — it cannot be accessed from outside.
bullets: Local variable: declared inside a method — created when the method starts, destroyed when it ends
You cannot access a local variable from outside the method that declared it
Two methods can each have a local variable with the same name — they are independent copies
Scope limits visibility intentionally — it prevents distant code from interfering with local state

slides.title: Block Scope & Common Mistakes
slides.content: A variable declared inside {} braces only lives within those braces — declaring inside a loop or if limits its scope.
bullets: A for loop counter (int i = 0) exists only inside that loop's body — i is gone after the closing brace
Declaring a variable inside an if block: it disappears after the if closes
Fix: declare the variable before the block if you need to read it afterwards
Scope bugs produce 'cannot find symbol' compile errors — check where the variable was declared

slides.title: Project: Bank Account Simulator
slides.content: Build a console bank account using separate methods for deposit, withdraw, and balance check.
bullets: Three operations: deposit (add to balance), withdraw (subtract if sufficient funds), checkBalance (display)
Each operation becomes its own method — main() just orchestrates calls and holds the balance variable
Pass balance in as a parameter and return the updated value — keeps side effects explicit
This project applies methods, parameters, return types, and conditional logic all together

slides.title: Menu-Driven Bank Loop
slides.content: Wrap the account operations in a do-while menu loop for an interactive session.
bullets: Use a do-while so the menu displays at least once before any condition is checked
Enhanced switch on choice routes each menu option to the correct method call
Update balance with the return value: balance = deposit(balance, amount); — captures the new total
This do-while + switch + methods pattern is the standard interactive console program structure

slides.title: Challenge — Transaction History
slides.content: Extend the bank account to log every deposit and withdrawal in a String array.
bullets: Declare String[] transactions = new String[20]; and int txCount = 0; before the loop
Inside deposit: transactions[txCount++] = String.format("Deposit:  +$%.2f", amount);
Inside withdraw (success only): transactions[txCount++] = String.format("Withdraw: -$%.2f", amount);
Add menu option 5 to print all recorded transactions with a for loop from 0 to txCount
